opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about it in layers, and I usually start with biology, because nature has already solved this problem and the solution is a strange one.

In vision you have three color receptors and a nice, low-dimensional physical stimulus: wavelength. Smell is completely different. Humans have roughly 400 kinds of olfactory receptors, and the stimulus is chemical structure, which has no obvious coordinate system. There's no "wavelength of smell." So the first architectural question is how you represent a molecule so a model can reason about it the way the nose does.

For us, the answer was graph neural networks. A molecule is naturally a graph: atoms are nodes and bonds are edges. Graph neural networks let you learn directly on that structure instead of hand-engineering chemical descriptors. We trained these models on expert-labeled odor data, with descriptors like "fruity," "woody," and "garlicky." What came out was what we called a principal odor map, an embedding space where molecules that smell alike sit near each other, even when they look structurally quite different. That's the exciting part, because it means the model learned something about perception, not just chemistry.

The second layer is evaluation, which is harder than it sounds. You can't just check against a database, because human odor perception is noisy and subjective. So we ran careful psychophysics studies with trained panelists and compared the model to individual humans. The model's predictions were closer to the panel consensus than a typical individual panelist was. To me that was the moment it felt like a real map, not just a curve fit.

The third layer, and the one I care most about now, is closing the loop with the physical world. Representation is only half of it. You need ways to sense, to digitize a scent from a sample, and then eventually to reconstruct or synthesize it. That's what I mean by giving computers a sense of smell. It's a full pipeline: chemistry in, a perceptual representation in the middle, and action out, whether that's discovering a new molecule, detecting a disease marker, or finding a safer insect repellent.

So the short version is: graphs for the input, a learned perceptual embedding as the core abstraction, and rigorous human-grounded evaluation tying it all together. The architecture mirrors the problem. Smell is about molecules meeting receptors meeting a brain, and our models have to respect each of those interfaces.

r001.rationale: The response describes layers in an olfactory pipeline, but does not characterize it as a fleet of predictive models spanning different aspects of smell.

r002.rationale: The response does not use self-driving cars or coordinated vehicle models as an architectural analogy.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it, the architecture really starts with the biology, because the biology is weird. Vision, you have three photoreceptor types, and from those three dimensions you can reconstruct basically the whole visual world. Hearing, you've got a cochlea that's essentially doing a Fourier transform. Smell, you have about four hundred receptor types in humans, and in a mouse it's over a thousand. So the input space is enormously high-dimensional right out of the gate, and nobody really knows the full response profile of most of those receptors. Each one is a little bit promiscuous, each odorant hits a bunch of them, so you get this combinatorial code where an odor is a pattern of activation across hundreds of channels.

What that told us is that the problem isn't really a perception problem in the way a camera is. The problem is chemistry. A molecule shows up at your nose, and the question is: what does that molecule smell like? That's a mapping from molecular structure to perceptual description, and that's the thing we set out to learn.

So the first architectural decision is how you represent a molecule. We went with graph neural networks, because a molecule is literally a graph. Atoms are nodes, bonds are edges. You do message passing, each atom aggregates information from its neighbors, you do that a few rounds, and then you pool it into an embedding for the whole molecule. Then you have a readout layer that predicts odor descriptors, things like fruity, musky, grassy, a few hundred of those. We trained it on tens of thousands of molecules from perfumery datasets where expert panels had labeled them.

The thing that was surprising, and honestly I didn't expect it, is that the embedding the model learns turns out to be a genuinely useful map. We call it the principal odor map. If you embed molecules in that space, nearby molecules smell alike, even when the structures are quite different. And this matters because structure-odor relationships are notoriously brittle. You can take two molecules that are nearly identical, flip a stereocenter, and one smells like spearmint and the other smells like caraway. And you can take two molecules that look nothing alike and they both smell like musk. A chemist staring at the drawings can't predict it. The model gets a lot of those cases right.

The validation we did, which I'm really proud of, is we had a trained human panel smell hundreds of molecules they had never been exposed to, that weren't in any training set, and we compared the model's predictions to the panel's descriptions. The model did about as well as the median panelist did against the panel consensus. So it's at roughly human level on that task.

Now, the second part of the architecture that I think about a lot is that the map also predicts things we never trained it on. We never showed it anything about receptor activation, and yet the map organizes molecules in a way that correlates with how olfactory receptors respond. We never showed it anything about mosquito behavior, and yet it predicts which molecules repel mosquitoes. That's the tell that you've learned something real about the underlying structure of the domain, rather than just fitting the labels.

And then the last piece, which is where Osmo lives, is going the other direction. Once you have a map from structure to smell, you can invert it. You can say, here's a point in odor space, give me a molecule that lands there. Or, here's a smell, find me a molecule that reproduces it. So the architecture isn't just a classifier, it becomes a generative tool for the chemistry.

The way I summarize it is: the architecture is really a translation layer between the language of chemistry and the language of perception. The neural network is just the mechanism. The actual insight is that those two languages are translatable at all, which fifteen years ago a lot of people would have told you was not the case.

r001.rationale: The response describes a molecule-to-odor model and related predictions, but does not characterize olfactory intelligence as a fleet of predictive models spanning different aspects of smell.

r002.rationale: The response makes no analogy to the coordinated models used in self-driving cars.

astra-6.text:
I think about it as a series of transformations. You start with a molecule, which you can represent as a graph: atoms are nodes, bonds are edges. But that representation doesn’t directly tell you what the molecule smells like. You need to learn a mapping from molecular structure into perception.

A useful architecture for that is a graph neural network. It passes information between atoms and builds up a representation of the whole molecule. We train that representation to predict odor descriptions, things like floral, fruity, or woody. And the interesting part is the space in the middle: can it organize molecules so that things that smell similar are close together, even when their structures look quite different?

But that’s one layer of the problem. In the real world, you’re smelling mixtures, at different concentrations, over time. So I think of olfactory intelligence as connecting chemistry to perception and then perception to behavior. Predicting a label for a single molecule gives you a starting point; understanding what an odor means in context is a much broader challenge.

r001.rationale: The response describes a molecular graph model and broader smell challenges, but does not characterize olfactory intelligence as a fleet of predictive models spanning different aspects of smell.

r002.rationale: The response makes no comparison to the coordinated models used in self-driving cars.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about it as a translation problem between molecules and perception. On one side, you have the structure of a molecule. On the other, you have the experience of smelling it: does it smell floral, fruity, woody? And the relationship between those two things is surprisingly difficult to predict.

So a useful starting point is a model that takes a molecular graph and learns a representation that’s organized around smell. We call that a principal odor map. The idea is that molecules that smell similar should be nearby in that space, even if their chemical structures look quite different.

But that representation is a foundation, rather than the whole system. Real smells are mixtures, and perception depends on concentration and context. You want an architecture that can build on that map to predict what you’ll smell, reason about mixtures, and eventually work backward: given a smell you want to create, which molecules could produce it?

That’s how I think about olfactory intelligence: connecting the physical world of molecules to a representation you can use to predict, compare, and design smells.

r001.rationale: The response describes a principal odor map and capabilities built on it, but does not characterize olfactory intelligence as a fleet of predictive models.

r002.rationale: The response does not use self-driving cars or a coordinated fleet of models as an architectural analogy.
